(CNN) -- Madagascar's military handed over the reins of the island nation to opposition leader Andry Rajoelina on Wednesday, ending a two-month long political crisis -- but apparently creating a constitutional one. Andry Rajoelina is six years too young to be Madagascar's president under its constitution. Rajoelina, a former disc jockey turned mayor of Madagascar's capital, declared himself president of a transitional government and his supporters pledged to hold elections in two years. But Rajoelina, at 34, is six years too young to be president, according to the country's constitution. Also, the constitution says the head of parliament's upper house must call elections within two months if something happens to the president. Madagascar's former president, Marc Ravalomanana, ceded power to his military Tuesday after insisting over the weekend that he would remain in control. Analysts think Ravalomanana had little choice but to step down once he had lost much of the army's support. The African Union had warned that any power transfer aided by the military would amount to a coup d' etat. The Union has since removed any mention of a coup in its official communique and called on the transitional government to "comply scrupulously with the provisions of the constitution of Madagascar on interim arrangements." Monja Roindefo, the opposition-appointed prime minister, vigorously defended the week's developments on the island, located off the southeastern coast of Africa. "Well, we would like to define what is a coup," he told CNN on Wednesday. "A coup is a group of people or persons who takes the power on behalf of sovereignty, on behalf of the people ... when the representative democracy doesn't work anymore." "As you know, as stated, in the African Union charter, the people have the right to defend itself from an oppression or a dictatorship in Africa," he added. Roindefo said the new government will hold elections but has given itself two years to clean up the process.  Watch more from iReporters and Twitterers on the crisis » . "How could you make an election immediately?" he said. "We need to reform the electoral commission. ... So the 24 months that we have given ourselves is to prepare all these types of elections in order to build a genuine democratic country." The African Union also asked that all steps be taken to ensure the safety of the former president. The opposition leader had called for Ravalomanana's arrest, accusing him of corruption, financial mismanagement and dictatorship. Ravalomanana was first elected in 2001 and won a second term in 2006. To many Malagasy, he represented a new breed of politician -- a self-made millionaire, a no-nonsense business leader. But Ravalomanana maintained his business empire while in office and it was unclear to many where his business interests ended and his political leadership began. His recent purchase of a $60 million airplane further stoked public discontent. Opposition leader Rajoelina was quick to seize on the sentiments and made fiery appeals to the country's impoverished masses. The country was plunged into political instability in January after thousands of people took to the streets to protest rising food prices and what they perceived as autocratic behavior by Ravalomanana. The protests soon degenerated into rioting and looting, and left about 100 people dead.  Watch more on president's resignation » . Soon after, Rajoelina declared that he was in charge of the country. He gave Ravalomanana until early February to step down. The president responded by firing Rajoelina as mayor of the capital, inciting the latter's supporters to once again descend on the streets. More deadly violence followed. Clashes spread to most provincial capitals and other cities across the country, with homes and businesses looted and burned, the U.S. State Department reported. CNN's David McKenzie contributed to this report.

At 34, Rajoelina is six years too young to serve as Madagascar’s president under the country’s constitution. A former disc jockey who became mayor of Madagascar’s capital, he declared himself president of a transitional government, while his supporters pledged to hold elections within two years.

The constitution also stipulates that, if something happens to the president, the head of Parliament’s upper house must call elections within two months.

Madagascar’s former president, Marc Ravalomanana, ceded power to the military on Tuesday after insisting over the weekend that he would remain in control. Analysts believe Ravalomanana had little choice but to step down once he had lost the support of much of the army.

The African Union had warned that any transfer of power aided by the military would amount to a coup d’état. It has since removed any reference to a coup from its official communiqué and called on the transitional government to “comply scrupulously with the provisions of the constitution of Madagascar on interim arrangements.”

Monja Roindefo, the opposition-appointed prime minister, vigorously defended the week’s developments on the island, which lies off Africa’s southeastern coast.

“Well, we would like to define what is a coup,” he told CNN on Wednesday. “A coup is a group of people or persons who takes the power on behalf of sovereignty, on behalf of the people ... when the representative democracy doesn’t work anymore.”

“As you know, as stated, in the African Union charter, the people have the right to defend itself from an oppression or a dictatorship in Africa,” he added.

Roindefo said the new government would hold elections but had given itself two years to reform the process.

*Watch more from iReporters and Twitterers on the crisis »*

“How could you make an election immediately?” he said. “We need to reform the electoral commission. ... So the 24 months that we have given ourselves is to prepare all these types of elections in order to build a genuine democratic country.”

The African Union also called for all necessary measures to ensure the former president’s safety. Rajoelina had called for Ravalomanana’s arrest, accusing him of corruption, financial mismanagement and dictatorship.

Ravalomanana was first elected in 2001 and won a second term in 2006. To many Malagasy, he represented a new breed of politician: a self-made millionaire and a no-nonsense business leader. However, he maintained his business empire while in office, leaving many uncertain about where his commercial interests ended and his political leadership began. His recent purchase of a $60 million airplane further fueled public discontent.

Rajoelina quickly capitalized on that sentiment, making fiery appeals to the country’s impoverished masses.

Madagascar was plunged into political instability in January after thousands of people took to the streets to protest rising food prices and what they perceived as Ravalomanana’s autocratic behavior. The demonstrations soon descended into rioting and looting, leaving about 100 people dead.

*Watch more on the president’s resignation »*

Soon afterward, Rajoelina declared that he was in charge of the country and gave Ravalomanana until early February to step down. The president responded by dismissing Rajoelina as mayor of the capital, prompting Rajoelina’s supporters to return to the streets.

(CNN) — Madagascar’s armed forces transferred control of the country to opposition figure Andry Rajoelina on Wednesday. The move brought a two-month political standoff to an end, while raising a new constitutional dispute.

Under Madagascar’s constitution, a president must be at least 40 years old. Rajoelina, 34, therefore falls six years short of the required age. The former disc jockey, who later became mayor of the capital, named himself head of a transitional administration, and his allies promised elections within two years.

That timetable also appears to conflict with the constitution. It stipulates that if the president can no longer serve, the leader of parliament’s upper chamber must call an election within two months.

Former President Marc Ravalomanana transferred authority to the military on Tuesday, despite having insisted during the previous weekend that he intended to remain in power. Analysts said his departure became largely unavoidable after he lost the backing of much of the army.

The African Union had cautioned that a military-assisted change of government would be considered a coup d’état. It later removed references to a coup from its formal statement and instead urged the interim administration to follow Madagascar’s constitutional rules governing transitional arrangements “scrupulously.”

Monja Roindefo, appointed prime minister by the opposition, strongly defended the week’s events in the Indian Ocean nation, which lies off Africa’s southeastern coast.

Speaking to CNN on Wednesday, Roindefo questioned how a coup should be defined. He argued that when representative democracy ceases to function, people may assume power in the name of popular sovereignty. He also cited the African Union charter, saying Africans have the right to protect themselves against oppression or dictatorship.

Roindefo said elections would take place, but maintained that the new authorities needed two years to overhaul the system first. He argued that voting could not be organized immediately because the electoral commission required reform. According to him, the 24-month period would allow the government to prepare the various elections needed to establish a genuinely democratic state.

More coverage of the crisis was available through iReport and Twitter contributors.

The African Union also called for every necessary measure to be taken to protect Ravalomanana. Rajoelina had demanded the former president’s arrest, alleging corruption, poor financial management and dictatorial conduct.

Ravalomanana was initially elected in 2001 and secured another term in 2006. Many Malagasy citizens saw him as representing a different kind of political leader: a self-made millionaire with a direct, business-oriented style. However, he continued running his commercial empire while serving as president, leaving many people uncertain about where his private business interests stopped and his public leadership began. Public anger intensified after he recently purchased an airplane for $60 million.

Rajoelina quickly capitalized on that dissatisfaction, directing impassioned messages toward Madagascar’s poor population.

The political turmoil began in January, when thousands demonstrated against higher food prices and what they regarded as Ravalomanana’s increasingly authoritarian conduct. The demonstrations soon turned into riots and looting, resulting in roughly 100 deaths.

Additional coverage focused on the president’s resignation.

Not long afterward, Rajoelina proclaimed that he had taken charge of the country and gave Ravalomanana until early February to resign. Ravalomanana answered by removing Rajoelina from his position as mayor of the capital. That decision prompted Rajoelina’s supporters to return to the streets, and further fatal violence followed.

According to the U.S. State Department, confrontations expanded to most provincial capitals and other cities throughout Madagascar. Homes and businesses were looted and set ablaze.

CNN’s David McKenzie contributed to the report.

**Madagascar military transfers power to opposition leader**

**ANTANANARIVO, Madagascar —** Madagascar’s military has transferred power to opposition leader Andry Rajoelina after President Marc Ravalomanana stepped down amid weeks of political unrest.

Ravalomanana resigned Tuesday, March 17, 2009, and handed authority to a military directorate. Senior officers, however, quickly transferred control to Rajoelina, the former mayor of Antananarivo who had led mass protests against the president.

Rajoelina, 34, declared himself head of a transitional government and pledged to organize elections within two years. His rise followed a prolonged confrontation that left more than 100 people dead and brought the Indian Ocean island’s government to a standstill.

Supporters of Rajoelina celebrated in the capital, while critics described the transfer as a military-backed coup. Rajoelina was below the constitutionally required age of 40 to serve as president.

The African Union condemned the change of power as unconstitutional and suspended Madagascar from the organization. International officials called for a peaceful return to constitutional rule.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the political crisis in Madagascar that brought Andry Rajoelina to power, including the constitutional concerns about his age and the military’s role.
counterfactuals.output:
Madagascar’s 2009 political crisis grew out of a confrontation between President **Marc Ravalomanana** and **Andry Rajoelina**, the young mayor of Antananarivo.

### How the crisis developed

Ravalomanana had faced growing criticism for concentrating political and economic power, restricting opposition media, and pursuing controversial projects, including a proposed large land lease to South Korea’s Daewoo Logistics. Rajoelina emerged as the leading opposition figure after the government closed a television station he owned in late 2008.

In January 2009, Rajoelina organized large demonstrations and declared that Ravalomanana’s government had lost legitimacy. Rioting and looting followed. The confrontation worsened on **7 February**, when presidential security forces fired on opposition demonstrators approaching the presidential palace, killing dozens.

Rajoelina then proclaimed a rival transitional administration. The government removed him as mayor, but protests continued and the security forces began to fracture.

### The military’s decisive role

In March, soldiers at the **CAPSAT** camp near Antananarivo mutinied, saying they would no longer obey orders to suppress civilians. Elements of the armed forces then openly supported Rajoelina, replaced senior commanders, and took control of key government institutions. Although the crisis involved mass protests, this military shift was what made Ravalomanana’s position untenable.

On **17 March 2009**, Ravalomanana resigned and purported to transfer presidential authority to a military directorate headed by Vice Admiral Hippolyte Ramaroson. The military leadership almost immediately transferred authority to Rajoelina, who became head of a **High Transitional Authority**. Madagascar’s High Constitutional Court subsequently recognized the transfer, but many domestic opponents and foreign governments regarded that recognition as legal cover for a military-backed change of power.

### Constitutional concerns, including Rajoelina’s age

The transfer did not follow the constitution’s normal presidential-succession procedure. In the event of a vacancy, authority was supposed to pass temporarily to designated civilian institutions—principally the president of the Senate, or under some circumstances the government collectively—followed by an election. The constitution did not provide for the outgoing president to hand power to a military directorate, nor for that directorate to appoint a new national leader.

There was also a clear age problem. Rajoelina was **34 years old** in March 2009, while the constitution required a presidential candidate to be at least **40**. His supporters argued that he was not assuming an ordinary elected presidential term but leading an exceptional transitional authority. Critics replied that changing his title did not remove the constitutional defect, because he was exercising the powers of the presidency without meeting its qualifications or being elected.

A later constitution adopted in 2010 lowered the minimum presidential age to **35**, but that did not retroactively resolve the legality of the 2009 takeover.

### International reaction

The **African Union**, the Southern African Development Community, and many foreign governments characterized the event as an **unconstitutional change of government**, commonly described as a military-backed coup. Madagascar was suspended from regional bodies and faced diplomatic isolation and reductions in foreign aid. The transition lasted for several years before elections restored a formally elected government in 2014.

In short, Rajoelina rose through a genuine popular and political revolt against Ravalomanana, but his actual accession depended on the armed forces abandoning the president and transferring power outside the constitution. His being below the constitutional minimum age further reinforced the view that the new regime was extra-constitutional.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news article on the 2009 Madagascar power transfer, covering the African Union’s response, plans for elections, and accusations against former President Ravalomanana.
counterfactuals.output:
# Madagascar’s 2009 Power Transfer Draws African Union Condemnation and Election Pledges

**ANTANANARIVO, Madagascar —** Madagascar entered a prolonged political crisis in March 2009 after President Marc Ravalomanana resigned and the military transferred authority to opposition leader Andry Rajoelina, a move the African Union condemned as an unconstitutional change of government.

The transfer followed weeks of demonstrations, deadly clashes and a widening mutiny within the armed forces. Ravalomanana announced on March 17 that he was handing presidential powers to a senior military directorate. Military leaders, however, quickly passed control to Rajoelina, the former mayor of Antananarivo who had led a campaign demanding the president’s removal.

Rajoelina, then 34, assumed power as head of a transitional authority. His installation bypassed the constitutional line of succession, under which authority would ordinarily have passed to the president of the Senate. Rajoelina was also below the constitutionally required minimum age of 40 for a president.

Ravalomanana’s supporters said he had been forced from office by the military and described the change as a coup. Rajoelina and his allies maintained that the president had lost legitimacy through repression, corruption and abuse of state institutions.

## African Union suspends Madagascar

The African Union’s Peace and Security Council rejected the transfer, saying it violated Madagascar’s constitution and the AU’s rules against military coups and other unconstitutional seizures of power.

On March 20, the organization suspended Madagascar from participation in AU activities. It called for the restoration of constitutional government and warned those involved in the transfer that sanctions could follow if an agreed political settlement was not reached.

AU officials emphasized that a president’s departure could not be used to justify handing power to an unelected opposition movement through military intervention. The organization later joined the United Nations, the Southern African Development Community and other international mediators in seeking negotiations among Madagascar’s competing political factions.

SADC took an especially critical position, refusing to recognize Rajoelina’s government and calling for the return of constitutional order. International donors also froze or reduced some non-humanitarian assistance, increasing pressure on an economy already weakened by the unrest.

Rajoelina rejected the description of the transition as a coup, arguing that Ravalomanana had formally resigned and that the military had acted to prevent chaos. Critics countered that the resignation took place after mutinous troops seized key state institutions and made clear that they would no longer obey the president.

## Elections promised, but timetable uncertain

The transitional government said its principal task would be to revise the constitution and organize elections. Rajoelina initially promised a presidential vote within about two years and said the transition would not become a permanent government.

Officials later discussed a sequence that included a constitutional referendum, legislative elections and a presidential election. One early calendar contemplated a referendum in 2009, parliamentary voting in 2010 and a presidential contest later that year. The dates, however, were repeatedly disputed and delayed as opposition groups challenged the transitional authority’s legitimacy and demanded an inclusive agreement.

A central question was whether Rajoelina and other former presidents would be permitted to stand. Mediators argued that credible elections required neutral institutions, an agreed electoral framework and participation by the country’s principal political movements.

Negotiations eventually broadened to include Ravalomanana, Rajoelina and former presidents Didier Ratsiraka and Albert Zafy. Although several power-sharing arrangements were proposed during 2009, implementation repeatedly stalled over cabinet posts, control of security institutions and the conditions under which exiled leaders could return.

## Accusations against Ravalomanana

Rajoelina built his campaign around allegations that Ravalomanana had become increasingly authoritarian and had blurred the line between public office and his extensive business interests.

Before entering politics, Ravalomanana created the Tiko food and dairy conglomerate, which grew into one of Madagascar’s most powerful private enterprises. Opponents accused his administration of granting favorable treatment to companies linked to him and of using state resources and media regulation to weaken competitors. Ravalomanana denied corruption and said his business background had helped him promote economic growth.

His critics also pointed to the government’s purchase of a presidential aircraft, reportedly costing about $60 million, as evidence of wasteful spending in one of the world’s poorest countries. The acquisition became a potent political symbol and contributed to tensions with foreign donors.

The gravest allegations concerned the deaths of protesters on February 7, 2009. Security forces opened fire near the presidential palace in Antananarivo after a crowd moved toward a restricted area. Dozens were killed or wounded, although casualty estimates varied.

Rajoelina’s supporters accused Ravalomanana of ordering or authorizing the shooting. Ravalomanana disputed responsibility, and the exact chain of command remained contested. The incident nevertheless intensified public anger, weakened the president’s position and accelerated defections within the military.

Ravalomanana, in turn, accused Rajoelina of exploiting unrest and collaborating with mutinous soldiers to overthrow an elected government. After leaving office, he went into exile in southern Africa and continued to assert that he remained Madagascar’s legitimate president.

The 2009 transfer left the island nation internationally isolated and deeply divided. While the new authorities promised elections and democratic reforms, the African Union and other mediators insisted that voting alone would not resolve the crisis unless it followed an inclusive, constitutionally grounded political settlement.

**BREAKING NEWS: Madagascar president resigns after two-month political crisis**

**ANTANANARIVO, Madagascar — March 17, 2009** — Madagascar’s President Marc Ravalomanana resigned Tuesday after nearly two months of violent protests and transferred his authority to the military, which quickly handed power to opposition leader Andry Rajoelina.

Rajoelina, the former mayor of Antananarivo, announced a transitional government and said elections would be held within two years. The move capped a bitter struggle that began in January, when Rajoelina accused Ravalomanana of authoritarian rule, corruption and misuse of public resources.

The crisis brought repeated demonstrations, looting and clashes with security forces. More than 100 people were reported killed. In the deadliest single confrontation, presidential guards opened fire on opposition supporters near the presidential palace on February 7, killing at least 28 people.

Ravalomanana’s loss of military support proved decisive. He said he was stepping down and transferring power to a military directorate, but senior officers rejected that arrangement and backed Rajoelina instead.

Supporters of Rajoelina described the transfer as a popular uprising against an increasingly isolated president. Critics called it a military-backed coup. Rajoelina was 34—below the constitutionally required presidential age of 40—and had not won a national election.

Madagascar’s Constitutional Court later recognized Rajoelina as head of the transitional authority, giving the new administration a measure of domestic legal cover. Internationally, however, the African Union and other governments condemned the change as an unconstitutional transfer of power.

The immediate security situation remained tense as the transitional government sought to establish control and answer mounting questions about elections, constitutional rule and accountability for the deaths during the protests.
